newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU suspends planned wheat export tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU suspends planned wheat export tax.

text.p: The European Commission, faced with French opposition, on Wednesday suspended plans to tax wheat exports, leaving it uncertain whether the move will now go ahead, a European Commission official said.

The tax had been aimed at saving scarce supplies for EU domestic consumers and dampening prices which had surged on concern over world crop prospects following frost in the United States and dry weather in Europe.

But EU sources said French EU commissioner Edith Cresson objected, saying the tax was no longer needed because world wheat prices had since fallen and there was no longer a danger of an exodus of European wheat abroad.

Some EU sources noted that France was in the middle of an election campaign where the farm vote is important. The first round of legislative elections will be held on May 25 and the second and final round a week later.

Unanimity among the 20 EU commissioners was required to adopt the proposal for taxes of 15 Ecus a tonne on exports of soft wheat grain and 20 Ecus a tonne on wheat flour under a so-called written procedure.
"It's suspended, there's no new deadline," the Commission official said. "It can be reopened but it's not sure. We don't know what will happen now."
Exporters who have taken out special "nil value" licences to export wheat will be liable to tax if they have not customs-cleared their grain and flour exports before the tax is approved.

The official said the EU's cereals management committee, made up of delegates from member states, would discuss the question of an export tax at their next meeting on May 15, but a final decision was up to the Commission.
Meanwhile the Commission would continue to reject all requests for wheat export licences.

On April 24, the committee supported the proposed tax, although France, Germany and Austria voted against and three other countries abstained. A week earlier the EU had closed a weekly tender for this season's wheat exports, several weeks earlier than usual.

The EU started 1996/97 with a wheat export tax when stocks were low and prices high, but restored export subsidies in September when the prospect of bumper crops in the main producer countries dampened world prices.

French grain traders on Wednesday largely shrugged off the news that the planned export tax had been suspended, and said the move -- though unexpected -- would make little difference to the wheat market.
